headline: Scientists find air around a faraway planet

sources.title: Potential Atmosphere Detected on Habitable-Zone Exoplanet LHS 1140b
Astronomers spot first atmosphere around a potentially habitable alien world
Rocky Planet 48 Light-Years Away May Be First in a Habitable Zone With a Confirmed Atmosphere
Atmosphere Confirmed Around Habitable Zone Planet LHS 1140b (video, Anton Petrov)

chunks.text: Scientists have {{picked up}} the first signs of air around a small, rocky planet outside our [[solar system]]. The planet, called LHS 1140 b, sits about 48 [[light-years]] from Earth. It circles its star in the zone where the temperature could be right for water. This is [[a huge deal]], because a planet needs air to {{hold on to}} heat and to give life a chance. But the discovery did not {{end up}} being simple.

verbs.why: A microphone can pick up a faint sound, and a doctor can pick up small signs of illness during a checkup. Scientists picked up the first signs of air around a small, rocky planet 48 light-years from Earth.

verbs.correct: To keep something and not lose it
verbs.wrong: To pull heat in from a star
verbs.why: You hold on to a good memory long after it happens, and you hold on to your savings for hard times. A planet needs air to hold on to heat, or its surface stays too cold for life.

verbs.correct: To be in a situation in the end
verbs.wrong: To prove an idea was correct
verbs.why: A simple trip can end up taking all day, and a small argument can end up lasting for weeks. This discovery did not end up being simple, since the signal later vanished completely.

chunks.text: LHS 1140 b is a [[super-Earth]], which means it is rocky like Earth but much bigger. To study it, a team at Harvard University {{set out}} to watch the planet with a powerful [[telescope]] in Chile. In 2024, they {{came across}} [[helium]] [[gas]] escaping from the top of the planet's air. The planet's star {{gives off}} strong [[radiation]], and this slowly {{strips away}} the gas. For the scientists, it was a rare [[privilege]] to [[witness]] this so far from Earth.

verbs.correct: To start trying to do something
verbs.wrong: To aim a telescope at a planet
verbs.why: Explorers set out to cross a mountain range, and a student can set out to learn a new language. A team at Harvard set out to watch LHS 1140 b with a powerful telescope in Chile.
You might come across an old letter in a drawer, or come across a stray cat on your street. In 2024 the team came across helium gas escaping from the top of the planet's air.

verbs.correct: To release light, heat, or gas
verbs.wrong: To slowly grow dark and die
verbs.why: A hot stove gives off heat, and a scented candle gives off a strong smell. The planet's star gives off strong radiation that slowly damages the atmosphere below.

verbs.wrong: To pull something in with gravity
verbs.why: Wind and rain can strip away paint from an old fence, and stress can strip away someone's confidence over time. Here the star's radiation slowly strips away helium gas from the top of the planet's air.

chunks.text: In a surprising [[twist]], the [[signal]] [[did not last]]. When the team {{went back}} to check the planet in 2025, the helium had completely disappeared. Scientists think the air may [[shift]] and change [[over time]], which is why the signal appeared and then [[vanished]]. [[For now]], the change is a [[mystery]]. The team is not [[certain]] what happened, and more work is needed to {{find out}} what is {{going on}}.

verbs.correct: To return to a place or time
verbs.why: You go back to a favorite restaurant, or go back to your hometown for the holidays. When the team went back to check the planet in 2025, the helium signal had completely disappeared.

verbs.correct: To learn something you did not know
verbs.wrong: To solve a problem by thinking
verbs.why: You call a friend to find out how their trip went, or check the mail to find out if a package arrived. Scientists still need more work to find out why the helium signal appeared and then vanished.

verbs.correct: To be taking place right now
verbs.wrong: To continue to the next study
verbs.why: You ask a friend what is going on when they seem upset, and neighbors wonder what is going on during a loud party next door. Right now scientists are not sure what is going on with the planet's disappearing air.

chunks.text: To {{clear up}} the mystery, the team will {{take on}} a bigger study with the James Webb Space Telescope, the most powerful space telescope ever built. Their main goal is to {{track down}} water, which would [[prove]] the air is real. If they {{pull off}} this hard job and [[succeed]], LHS 1140 b could become [[one of the best]] places to look for life. Scientists around the world will follow the results [[closely]].

verbs.why: A good explanation can clear up confusion after a mix-up, and a phone call can clear up a misunderstanding fast. To clear up the mystery of the disappearing signal, the team will run a much bigger study.

verbs.correct: To begin to handle a task
verbs.wrong: To pay for a space mission
verbs.why: A new manager might take on extra staff, and a runner can take on a longer race after months of training. The team will take on a much bigger study using the James Webb Space Telescope.

verbs.wrong: To measure the amount of water
verbs.why: Detectives track down a missing car, and fans track down rare concert tickets online. The team's main goal now is to track down water, which would prove the planet's air is real.

verbs.wrong: To barely finish before the deadline
verbs.why: A small team can pull off a big win against the odds, and a chef can pull off a fancy dinner with little time. If scientists pull off this difficult search, LHS 1140 b could become one of the best places to look for life.

mainIdea.s: Scientists picked up signs of air on a distant rocky planet, but the signal vanished when they went back to check. They now plan a bigger study to find out if real air is there.
mainIdea.why: The team found helium escaping from the planet in 2024, but the signal had vanished by 2025. They now plan a bigger study with a powerful telescope to track down water.

mainIdea.s: Scientists have proven that a distant rocky planet holds a stable layer of air that can support life. Their next step, they say, is only to learn more about the planet's size and shape.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the article never says the air was proven or stable. The helium signal disappeared, and the team is not certain what happened.

mainIdea.s: Astronomers announced this year that they found a brand new rocky planet in a far off solar system. Thick clouds and intense heat make this new world a poor place to search for life.
mainIdea.why: This is about a different planet and a different discovery. The real story is about LHS 1140 b and a helium signal that appeared and then vanished.

lines.text: Astronomers {{picked up}} signs of air around a rocky planet 48 light-years away. A first for a planet that small.
Yes. The planet, a super-Earth, circles its star in the zone where water could exist. A Harvard team {{set out}} to watch it with a telescope in Chile.
In 2024 they {{came across}} helium escaping from the top of the atmosphere. The star {{gives off}} strong radiation that slowly {{strips away}} the gas.
[[Talk about luck]]. So the planet is losing its air?
[[Here's the twist]]. When the team {{went back}} in 2025, the helium had completely disappeared.
Nobody knows. The atmosphere may shift over time, and scientists need more work to {{find out}} what's {{going on}}.
So how do they {{clear up}} the mystery?
They'll {{take on}} a bigger study with the James Webb telescope. The goal is to {{track down}} water, which would prove the air is real.
Then this planet becomes one of the best places to look for life. A planet needs air to {{hold on to}} heat, so everything depends on it.
A vanishing atmosphere on a world we can barely see. [[What a time to be alive]].
